title: Shabari's Berries
hookLine: an old woman waits years for Rama with a basket of fruit
carry: bhakti: God accepts what's offered with love
tomorrow: why does Nani count 108 beads every morning?

lines: AN OLD WOMAN IN THE FOREST.
cards: Deep in the forest, an old woman named Shabari has been waiting for years. Her teachers, the sages of the hermitage, told her before they left this world that Rama would come.
So every day she gathers fruit and keeps watch. Then one day two young men walk up the path, dusty from the road: Rama, and his brother Lakshmana.

teach.b: In Valmiki's Ramayana she bows, welcomes them and offers what she has gathered: forest fruit. In later tellings, loved across India, she does something no host is supposed to do.
She bites each berry first, to check it's sweet, and offers Rama only the good ones, already tasted. Lakshmana flinches.
Rama eats every one, and says nothing has ever tasted sweeter. Feel it for a second: the tart skin, the juice, the mark of her teeth. By the rules of purity, those berries are spoiled.

teach.h: A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.
teach.b: This is bhakti, loving devotion, and Krishna puts it in one line of the Gita: whoever offers me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with love, I accept it.

The word there for fruit is phala, the same word that's in Nani's line: never to the fruits, ma phaleshu. Put the two lines side by side and the week clicks. You don't cling to the fruit of your work.
You offer it. Bhakti is why a Hindu home shrine gets the first of the food, a flower, a lamp, a spoonful of water, before anyone eats.
What comes back is prasad, food God has received, shared as a blessing. The gift is never measured by its price.
It's measured by the love in the hand. Tonight Priya copies phaleshu, and its letters wear their vowels like Shabari's berries wear her bite: an e on top, a u hanging below.

how: In many Hindu homes food is offered at the shrine before the meal and then shared as prasad; Shabari's berries are often told to children to show that the love counts more than the gift.

o: the script where phala, fruit, is written फल
the plate offered at the home shrine

games.q: the forest offering — tap the pairs.
p: food offered to God, then shared

s: Rama refused the berries because they'd been bitten
in the tellings, he eats every one and says nothing tasted sweeter.
in the Gita, Krishna accepts even a leaf or a little water offered with love
a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water: it's the love that's offered.
the bitten berries come from Valmiki's Ramayana
Valmiki has Shabari offer forest fruit; the tasting is from later tellings loved across India.

games.q: your friend at dinner asks why your mom puts a little of everything on a plate for the home shrine before anyone eats. what do you say?
o: it's an offering, like Shabari's fruit: God gets it first, and what comes back is prasad.
it's so the gods don't get angry and spoil the meal.
it's an old habit; nobody believes in it anymore.
games.why: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, offered with love: that's bhakti. the food that comes back is prasad, a blessing.

practice: If there's fruit or anything to eat or drink nearby, take one small piece.

Before you eat it, pause and offer it: if you pray, hold it a moment and offer it to God in your own words, the way many Hindus offer food before a meal; if you don't, think of who grew it and carried it to you.
Then taste it slowly, all the way through.

wordCard.voice: Devanagari: the script of phala, fruit, the word that joins Shabari's basket to Nani's line.

orig.note: Sanskrit: fruit. The phala of Krishna's leaf, flower and fruit, and of phaleshu, 'in the fruits', in Nani's line.

carryVoice: Carry this: bhakti. God accepts a leaf, a flower, a fruit, offered with love. Rest well.
